title: What is known about 1RB1LC_1LA---_1LD0LA_1RE0LE_0RF1RE_1LB1RD
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LC_1LA---_1LD0LA_1RE0LE_0RF1RE_1LB1RD.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The right end of the tape is ... 1 0 1^P 0 (10)^Q 1^5. Lean proves the round (P, Q) → (P − 2, Q + 2) for every P ≥ 7, even Q ≥ 2 and every tape to the left, and k rounds by induction. When the ones are used up the phase end walks into the rest of the tape, which is an irregular mixture of short words that grows with every phase, and starts the next phase: often with P = 9, sometimes with P' = 2P + 11, and then again and again (a chain 37, 85, 181, ..., 3,145,717 of 16 doublings). 156 phases, more than 3·1013 steps, have been followed exactly without a halt. What decides the next phase: a phase end either reads at most a few dozen cells next to the block and gives P′ = 2P + c (the doublings), or crosses the whole tape left of the block and restarts with P′ in {9, 29, 41, 65, 169}; the long ends rewrite the left tape, and nothing regular has been found in what they leave.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (B1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 36,595 cells have been visited and 27,358 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: The round, and a phase of rounds by induction
claims.text: From L 1 0 1^(p+7) 0 (1010)^(q+1) 1^5 E> 0^inf the machine reaches L 1 0 1^(p+5) 0 (1010)^(q+2) 1^5 E> 0^inf in 28q+64 steps, for all p, q and every tape L; k rounds take (P + 2k, Q) to (P, Q + 2k) for P ≥ 5 and even Q ≥ 2.

claims.title: 156 phases without a halt
claims.text: py/phases.py runs the exact accelerated simulator py/tsim.py and skips the rounds of each phase by the Lean rule (only for even Q; the few phases with odd Q, where the rule does not apply and the run does something else, are simulated cell by cell). In 156 phases there is no halt; the largest phase has P = 3,145,717 and alone costs about 3.5·1013 steps.

claims.title: Doubling chains
claims.text: The phase starts have P = 9 in 69 of the 156 phases; otherwise P' = 2P + 11 follows a phase that ended next to the right words, giving chains such as 37, 85, 181, 373, ..., 3,145,717 (16 doublings), after which P drops back to a small value.

claims.title: What decides doubling or reset: how far the phase end reads
claims.text: For each of the first 36 phases the tape after the rounds was copied and the phase end run on it alone, recording how far left of the block the head goes. There are two kinds. Short ends read at most 56 cells and give P′ = 2P + c, with c set by those cells: the context 1110 11111 0 1010 (14 cells) gives c = 11 and leaves the same 14 cells again, which is why the doublings 37, 85, 181, ... repeat; other contexts give c = 27, 15, 19, 5, −11, 31, 19. Long ends cross the whole tape left of the block and run into the blank tape beyond (24 of the 36), and then P′ is 9, 29, 41, 65 or 169, whatever P was. So a phase doubles exactly when the few cells next to the block allow a short end; the long ends rewrite the whole left tape and are where its irregular words come from.

claims.title: Why it is hard
claims.text: What the next phase does depends on the cells next to the block (a short end, a doubling or near-doubling) or on the whole tape left of it (a long end, which crosses all of it and restarts with a small P). The long ends rewrite the left tape each time; no counter or regular structure has been found in what they leave.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Equivalent to: does some phase end ever bring the head to B reading 1, the only halting transition?

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. At the right end of the tape this machine runs a simple, provable loop that trades a block of ones for pairs 10; how the next block starts, small again or twice as large, depends on a jumble of cells further left that the machine keeps rewriting.

facts.text: Followed exactly, more than 3·10<sup>13</sup> steps, no halt.
The loop of a phase is proved in Lean for every size.
Phases can double the block, up to 16 times in a row so far.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.396).
After 109 steps the tape spans 36,595 cells (539 left of the start, 24,733 right), with a density of 1s of 0.748.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Rounds: two ones for two words
html: A phase starts when the head, in state E, reaches a new cell at the right end of

with Q = 2. In each round the head runs left over the (10)^Q block, takes two ones from the block of P ones and comes back, leaving two more words 10: (P, Q) → (P − 2, Q + 2) in 14Q + 36 steps (Lean: round, rounds). A phase with P ones costs about 3.5·P2 steps.

sections.heading: Double or reset
html: When the ones are used up the head walks into the tape further left. Sometimes it turns the (10)^Q block into the next block of ones, P' = 2P + 11; sometimes the phase restarts with P = 9 or another small value. Over 156 phases, P = 9 starts 69 of them, and the longest chain of doublings so far goes 37, 85, 181, 373, 757, 1,525, ..., 3,145,717.
Which happens is decided by the cells left of the block: a long, irregular mixture of short words such as 1^3 0, 1^7 0 and 1110 that the phase ends rewrite and that grows with the phases.

sections.heading: Where it could halt
html: The only halting transition is B reading 1. The rounds never halt (Lean), so a halt would come at a phase end, in the junk. Because the doubling chains make the phases exponentially long, simulation reaches far in steps but only a few hundred phases; understanding the junk is the next step.

family: doubling phases on a growing junk tape
summary: Phases at the right end: a block of P ones is traded two at a time for words 10, then the phase end either doubles P (P' = 2P + 11, up to 16 times in a row so far) or resets it, depending on the irregular tape it meets on its way left. Open.
